title: Obren on AI
basis: Reconstructed from config.yaml and all nine published index.md files and their accepted legacy spec.md files in reading order. There is no journal-level PLAN.md, _research directory, scenario ledger, or consistency-rulings file. Existing articles and their specs provide the factual and editorial baseline; the amplifier post also identifies its local PLAN.md. All three parts and all nine posts are specified in full before prose revision. Existing names, figures, dates, links, illustrations, and front matter are to be preserved; this run does not add or correct external factual claims.

know: How AI changes the scarce work in software delivery, model-powered products, and technology leadership.
believe: Cheaper artifact production increases the importance of intended outcomes, evaluation, human understanding, and accountable decisions.
can_do: Distinguish a generation problem from a problem of behavior, verification, product fit, ownership, or leadership, and choose a corresponding practice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can connect the journal's engineering, product, and leadership arguments without treating output volume as value.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What common problem links the software, product, and leadership notes, and how does each part respond?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Generation becomes cheaper while trustworthy outcomes still need explicit behavior, inspectable systems, evaluation of product fit, human understanding, and accountable decisions; the parts apply that reasoning to software, products, and leadership.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can choose a practical next step that addresses the limiting work in an AI initiative.
acceptance_criteria.probe: If an AI initiative produces impressive artifacts but does not deliver dependable value, what should you examine before generating more?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Check the intended outcome, the evidence and downstream bottleneck, human understanding and ownership, product fit, and decision authority; select a concrete practice such as a behavior spec, evaluation, stable seam, or bounded intent agreement.

audience.who: Software engineers, architects, product leaders, and technology leaders using AI to build systems or products and responsible for judging, maintaining, or leading the resulting work.
already_knows: The broad software lifecycle: designing, implementing, reviewing, testing, deploying, and maintaining a system.
That AI tools can generate code, documents, designs, and options, and that organizations must decide how to use their output.
Basic concepts such as a database, API, dependency, team responsibility, and a customer-facing product.
does_not_know: The journal's particular reactor, amplifier, Vibe Monolith, RISC, fashion, and leadership-ladder analogies.
The distinctions between structure and behavior, output and outcome, production and personal understanding, and AI-assisted development and model-powered products.
The studies, historical ideas, and attribution boundaries used to support these essays.

thesis.question: How can people turn cheaper AI-generated artifacts into value they can trust and sustain?
thesis.claim: As AI makes artifact production cheaper, teams must specify intended outcomes, make generated work inspectable, and retain human responsibility to verify that outputs meet user needs and continue to do so as models and systems change.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that organizations can capture most of AI's value by adopting better models and scaling output within their existing delivery, product, and leadership practices.
thesis.so_what: Teams should direct effort toward clear intent, evaluation, understandable systems, customer fit, and accountable choices instead of using output volume as the main sign of progress.
thesis.how_why: More output can outpace verification and comprehension, model changes can break product fit, and neither generated artifacts nor autonomous actions supply the contextual judgment and trust needed to own their consequences.

supporting_claims.claim: Trustworthy AI-assisted software requires explicit behavior, surrounding controls, human understanding, and manageable architecture and platform surfaces.
Model-powered products require repeated evaluation of changing material against a stable customer promise.
Human intent, bounded delegation, agency, judgment, and persuasion remain necessary to turn generated options into accountable action.

flow.rationale: The collection groups the argument by the responsibility under examination: first building and owning software, then preserving customer value when a model is part of the product, then leading the decisions and people involved. Software first establishes the outcome and verification problem; the product part distinguishes a change in product material from a change in production tools; leadership last turns the shared need for human responsibility into an operating practice and a personal learning agenda. Reordering would either blur the two AI uses before they are contrasted or give leadership prescriptions before the engineering and product decisions that motivate them. Each essay remains usable on its own, so cross-links are further reading rather than required prerequisites.

hook.content: When AI makes the artifact easy to produce, what work still determines the outcome?

opening.bridge: Use the familiar focus on software structure to expose the wider distinction between producing an artifact and achieving the effect it is meant to cause.
opening.roadmap: Move from intended behavior and trustworthy software to model-dependent product value, then to the leadership required to decide and act responsibly.

closing.synthesis: Specification and evaluation connect generated artifacts to intended effects only when people understand the work, choose in context, and bring others into the decision.
closing.so_what: The generation dividend becomes durable value through accountable action rather than an accumulating stock of artifacts.
closing.callback: The opening question of what remains when artifact production stops being the scarce work.

takeaway.content: Choose one real AI-assisted decision, make its intended outcome and limits explicit, test the options, and explain the chosen course to the people who must live with it.

non_goals.topic: A forecast of exact AI capabilities, adoption rates, or employment outcomes.
A universal model, toolchain, framework, or platform recommendation.
A claim that generation replaces expertise, evaluation, architecture, or human accountability.
A literal equivalence between AI and the physical or social systems used as essay analogies.
A policy manual for AI safety, security, governance, or autonomous-agent deployment.
Re-researching, correcting, or extending claims about real people, companies, products, prices, dates, or study figures during this outcome-revision run.
Rewriting companion summaries, dialogs, or comics in this run; their existing content and assets remain outside the requested article/spec pass.

open_questions: Should a later editorial pass create a shared evidence ledger and resolve source-density expectations for AI Notes? This run has no canonical ledger and preserves existing attribution and caveats.

The legacy structure-to-behavior spec leaves open whether the cross-discipline convergence argument needs an additional external witness. This run retains it as the author's argument without inventing evidence.

rejected: Pause for an additional approval already waived by the user.

rejected: Reorder existing published navigation to make a new book structure.

Require new evidence, new case studies, or exact recall of every cited figure.

decision_log.decision: Use the first and last existing essays as carriers of the journal opening and closing. They should make the artifact-to-outcome thread visible while remaining standalone essays; no new introduction or closing page is added.
The Product part has one essay supporting both of its claims: changing model material and evaluation against a stable promise. Its flow records that no internal post ordering decision exists.

Use existing articles and legacy specs as the factual baseline because no journal ledger exists. Preserve quotations, names, numerical claims, links, figures, and qualifications; any unresolved factual concerns remain questions for separate editorial work.

No numeric word limit was found in any of the nine legacy specs. Do not introduce a new cap or interpret reading-time metadata as a word limit; post workers should preserve the author's scale and avoid unnecessary expansion.
The user limits draft checking to at most two total rounds per post. Post-level revision must stop at that limit and report remaining failures or stale reports without implying a pass.

The isolated Software part thesis reviewer passed answer, dispute, and mechanism tests but asked for a concrete meaning of enough human understanding to own shipped work. The claim now names explaining behavior, evaluating changes, and responding to failures; its six post claims are unchanged.

The isolated amplifier thesis reviewer passed answer, dispute, and mechanism tests but found changes results and improve inputs too general. This retains both the conditional-effects and system-constraint strands of the published argument.

The isolated fashion thesis reviewer passed answer, dispute, and mechanism tests but found improve possibilities and regress product fit underspecified. The claim now names newly feasible workflows and broken behavior required by an existing customer job, preserving the non-monotonic upgrade argument.

All thirteen isolated thesis rubrics now pass. Four initial specificity failures (journal, Software part, amplifier, fashion) were revised and passed with fresh readers; nine passed unchanged. The fresh flow reader judged the journal and Software part sound with notes and the Product and Leadership parts sound, with no moves, merges, or cuts requested. Its sole scope note was taken by clarifying the reactor essay's role as production controls and the later product essay's role as changing customer workflows; reading order and thesis objects remain unchanged.

changelog.change: Created a draft outcome contract for the complete existing AI Notes journal: three full parts and nine full essays, with reader outcomes, disputable theses, supporting roles, flow, openings, closings, and transitions. Written before post spec conversion or prose revision in the user-authorized auto run.

know: How cheaper generation changes the work required to specify, verify, understand, and maintain software.
believe: Sustainable AI-assisted delivery depends on the surrounding engineering and human understanding, not output volume alone.
can_do: Identify whether a team's limiting work is behavioral clarity, verification, comprehension, unstable boundaries, or hidden platform behavior.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader connects intended behavior to verification and sustainable ownership rather than treating generated output as the result.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How do the six essays together explain a team that produces more code but cannot confidently own or release it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Clear behavior and outcomes define the target; surrounding checks establish evidence; bottlenecks and human comprehension constrain pace; stable seams and an inspectable platform make ownership tractable.

thesis.question: What lets teams sustain AI-assisted software development as generation becomes cheaper?
thesis.claim: Teams can sustain AI-assisted development by specifying intended behavior, limiting verification and comprehension burdens through stable boundaries and inspectable platforms, and retaining people who can explain shipped behavior, evaluate changes, and respond to failures.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that more capable agents and more automated tests will make increased code volume translate into sustainable delivery without changing specification, architecture, or ownership practices.
thesis.so_what: Engineering investment must address the work between producing code and taking responsibility for its behavior over time.
thesis.how_why: Generation lowers one cost while moving pressure to evaluation, integration, and understanding; explicit intent and deliberate limits on change and hidden behavior make those remaining costs manageable.

supporting_claims.claim: Cheaper structural production shifts attention to specifying behavior and outcomes across disciplines.
Controls, evaluation, workflows, and accountable operation turn model capability into trustworthy production use.
Task fit, standards, and delivery bottlenecks determine whether faster generation improves system outcomes.
People must build understanding of how generated work functions and whether it serves its context.
Stable architectural seams distribute ownership and reduce the human burden of continuous re-architecting.
Reduced platform surfaces improve inspectability only when evaluation and stewardship preserve the expertise and safeguards that matter.

role.contribution: Shows how to turn cheap generation into software people can evaluate, understand, and sustain.

flow.rationale: The first two essays establish what software must achieve and the systems that make it trustworthy; the next two explain the delivery and comprehension constraints; the final two show how stable seams and reduced hidden behavior address those constraints. Moving platform advice first would invite minimalism without a purpose, and moving the architectural response ahead of the comprehension problem would hide why stable boundaries matter to people. The opening is a broad orientation, not a claim that later essays are prerequisites for understanding it.

hook.content: If producing structure becomes cheap, what work still determines whether software serves its users?

opening.bridge: Begin with the familiar effort of designing and reviewing structure, then distinguish that artifact from the behavior and outcome it serves.
opening.roadmap: Follow the shift in scarce work from intended behavior, through surrounding controls and delivery constraints, to understanding and the architecture that supports ownership.

closing.synthesis: Explicit behavior and reviewable changes only remain useful when the platform keeps evaluation and human ownership possible as output grows.
closing.so_what: Teams can spend the generation dividend on work they can understand and maintain rather than accumulating an ever larger review burden.
closing.callback: The opening distinction between producing structure and achieving behavior users can rely on.

takeaway.content: Choose the smallest reliable platform for the intended behavior, retain the abstractions that carry needed expertise, and verify what is generated.

posts.title: From Structure to Behavior, From Output to Outcome
posts.question: What should become the central work of software disciplines when AI makes structure cheaper to produce?

know: Why structural design served as an early proxy for behavior, and how cheaper generation changes that trade-off.
How the move from structure to behavior parallels the product-management move from output to outcome.
believe: Product, design, architecture, and engineering can co-author intended outcomes and behavior while retaining distinct expertise.
Cheaper structural production increases the need for behavioral and structural judgment.
can_do: State an intended behavior and its outcome before asking an agent to generate a design.
Identify a handoff where one shared specification would preserve intent.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains the shared pattern behind structure-to-behavior and output-to-outcome, including why the old proxies were useful.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Why did engineers focus on structure, and how is the change described here related to product management moving from output to outcome?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The visible artifact was easier to inspect and costly to produce, so it stood in for the harder-to-observe effect; cheaper production shifts attention to behavior and outcomes and allows earlier observation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains how one shared specification can connect disciplines without making their expertise interchangeable.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What could product managers, designers, architects, and engineers share, and what would remain different about their contributions?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A structured specification connects customer outcomes, intended behavior, and constraints; the product-domain example makes this concrete, while each discipline retains its judgment and expertise.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can choose a practical change to review or specification work while preserving the need to judge generated structure.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What would you change in a design review after reading this, and why would generated architecture still need human attention?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Review intended behavior, edge cases, failures, and outcomes before or alongside structure; behavior remains hard to specify, verify, and agree on, and generated structure still affects operation, cost, and evolution.

thesis.question: What should become the central work of software disciplines when AI makes structure cheaper to produce?
thesis.claim: As AI makes structure cheaper to produce and behavior faster to observe, product, design, architecture, and engineering should co-author specifications of intended outcomes and behavior while retaining their distinct expertise.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that AI mainly accelerates each existing craft, so separate artifact ownership and sequential handoffs should remain the organizing model.
thesis.so_what: Teams should spend review effort on the behavior users need and preserve intent across disciplines instead of treating a completed diagram, feature, or codebase as evidence of value.
thesis.how_why: Structure was an inspectable proxy when construction delayed feedback; cheaper construction exposes the harder questions of what should happen and why, which every discipline must answer together.

role.contribution: Establishes what generated software must serve before the part addresses how teams can trust and maintain it.

posts.title: AI Is the Reactor, Not the Plant
posts.question: Where should teams direct engineering effort when a capable model is already available?

know: The difference between raw model capability and the surrounding systems that make it usable.
How control, channel, and contain map to AI engineering and why safeguards need layers.
believe: Trustworthy production use requires sustained investment around the model.
The reactor analogy explains surrounding work without equating AI risks with physical nuclear hazards.
can_do: Identify control, conversion, containment, and accountable ownership work missing from an AI plan.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader maps each of control, channel, and contain to a concrete AI practice and explains why a single safeguard is insufficient.
acceptance_criteria.probe: For an AI workflow, what would control, channel, and contain mean, and what does defense in depth add?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Control limits actions through scope, instructions, or permissions; channel turns outputs into checked results through evaluation or workflows; contain bounds failures through sandboxing, review, limits, or rollback; another layer must hold when one fails.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader uses the nuclear evidence directionally and can state the analogy's limits.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What does the nuclear cost evidence support, and what should you avoid inferring about AI from the analogy?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The surrounding plant accounts for substantial work and cost; attributed breakdowns with different bases are not universal ratios or AI budgets; AI has different hazards, changing behavior, and can have value without a production control system.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader identifies an engineering or organizational investment beyond choosing a more capable model.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What concrete change would this article suggest to the staffing, measurement, or ownership of an AI project?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Budget for evaluation and surrounding systems, define permissions and layered safeguards, measure conversion into correct results, or name the accountable human owner; connect the choice to trustworthy use.

thesis.question: Where should teams direct engineering effort when a capable model is already available?
thesis.claim: Teams seeking trustworthy production use should treat the model as one component and direct most engineering effort to the surrounding controls, evaluation, workflows, and accountable operation.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that selecting or training a sufficiently capable model solves most of the production problem, leaving integration and oversight as minor finishing work.
thesis.so_what: Project budgets, delivery plans, and ownership need to include the work that turns a convincing demonstration into a service people can rely on.
thesis.how_why: Raw generation does not itself constrain permitted actions, verify results, contain failures, or assign responsibility; those properties come from the systems around it, as the bounded reactor analogy illustrates.

role.contribution: Establishes the engineering controls and ownership for dependable production use, preparing for the later product essay's separate question of changing customer workflows.

transition_in.carries_over: Generating structure cheaply shifts attention to the behavior and outcomes it must serve.
transition_in.introduces: The surrounding controls and evaluation that make generated capability serve those intentions.

posts.title: AI Is an Amplifier, Not an Accelerator
posts.question: Why does AI adoption produce faster individuals without consistently producing faster or cheaper delivery?

know: Why AI effects vary with task, user, standards, and operating context rather than guaranteeing a uniform speedup.
Why cheaper generation can raise ownership costs and leave team throughput constrained.
believe: Measured system outcomes matter more than felt individual speed.
AI investment should improve the inputs and constraints that govern results.
can_do: Locate a likely bottleneck and choose what to measure before scaling AI use.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains the amplifier model, its evidence, and its limits without treating the arithmetic as a universal law.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What does the amplifier model explain about differing AI results, and where does the metaphor stop helping?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Effects depend on user, task, and context and can worsen results; the cited contrasting studies illustrate that variability; AI also adds capabilities and its gain varies rather than remaining one constant.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains how faster generation can coexist with unchanged or worse team delivery and higher ownership costs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team generates code faster but its review queue grows and releases do not improve. How does the article explain that result?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Improving a non-bottleneck adds work before the constraint; review, integration, legacy limits, and coordination can absorb local gains, while maintaining more code can offset generation savings.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader proposes a measured adoption move tied to the real bottleneck and the quality of inputs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Before expanding AI use, what would you measure or change, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Measure actual task and delivery outcomes rather than perception, examine downstream review and maintenance burden, strengthen standards or context, and address the limiting stage before scaling.

thesis.question: Why does AI adoption produce faster individuals without consistently producing faster or cheaper delivery?
thesis.claim: AI can improve or worsen task speed and correctness while increasing downstream review and maintenance work, so teams should measure those effects and address delivery bottlenecks before scaling generation.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that wider access to a more capable coding model will translate individual speed gains into broadly similar delivery and cost gains across teams.
thesis.so_what: Leaders need measured task and system outcomes to decide where to invest; otherwise they can expand review queues and maintenance bills while celebrating faster generation.
thesis.how_why: Capability varies across tasks, ownership costs sit downstream of generation, and a faster non-bottleneck cannot increase throughput beyond the stage that limits the delivery chain.

role.contribution: Explains why adding generation to the surrounding system can increase strain unless teams address its inputs and limiting stages.

transition_in.carries_over: A model becomes useful through the engineering and operating system around it.
transition_in.introduces: How that system determines whether more generation improves results or increases downstream strain.

posts.title: You Can Outsource Thinking. You Cannot Outsource Understanding.
posts.question: What must people retain when AI can produce the designs, code, and analyses they need?

know: The article's distinction between producing an artifact and personally understanding how it works and whether it serves a real need.
Why faster generation can leave human comprehension as the limiting step.
believe: Outsourcing production does not transfer ownership or understanding to the person receiving the result.
Active reconstruction and questioning can build understanding while passive acceptance does not ensure it.
can_do: Re-derive a generated design from a simple version, with each change motivated by a problem.
Test whether they can explain, change, and assess the value of generated work.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader distinguishes outsourced production from understanding how an artifact works and whether it serves its context.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An AI produces a correct-looking design. What two kinds of understanding must its human owner still develop, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How the design works well enough to explain, change, and debug it; whether it solves the real problem under local constraints. A produced artifact does not itself supply that personal grasp or accountable judgment.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains why faster generation can increase comprehension debt and separates passive delegation from active AI use.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Why can improving models leave humans more constrained, and what kind of AI use does the article caution against?
acceptance_criteria.expected: More artifacts arrive faster than people can understand and relate them to reality; accepting output passively can leave comprehension debt, while questioning and reconstructing it keeps humans engaged. The cited studies are cautions with their stated limits.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can describe the reconstruction method as a human learning path rather than a claim to reveal the model's internal reasoning.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How would you use the article's method to understand a generated design before owning it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Start with the simplest working version, expose one limitation, make one motivated design decision, and repeat; explain why each part exists and test its fit to the real need, without treating the story as the model's actual internal process.

thesis.question: What must people retain when AI can produce the designs, code, and analyses they need?
thesis.claim: People can delegate artifact production to AI, but must build their own understanding of how the result works and whether it serves a real need, using active questioning and stepwise reconstruction before taking ownership.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a correct generated artifact, accompanied by a fluent explanation, gives its recipient enough understanding to own it without further learning.
thesis.so_what: Teams need time and practices for comprehension, or the volume of generated work can grow beyond their ability to explain, maintain, and judge it.
thesis.how_why: Understanding connects causes, trade-offs, and local context in a person; generation increases artifact supply faster than human attention, while reconstruction makes each design choice answer a problem the learner has encountered.

role.contribution: Locates the human comprehension constraint that remains after teams improve generation and delivery mechanics.

transition_in.carries_over: A faster production stage can move the constraint to a slower stage that still needs attention.
transition_in.introduces: Human understanding as the constraint that artifact generation cannot remove on its recipient's behalf.

posts.title: Breaking Up the Vibe Monolith: Architecting AI-Built Systems to Keep Their Cool
posts.question: How can teams sustain AI-assisted development when the architecture changes faster than people can understand and own it?

know: How continuous re-architecting creates a Vibe Monolith even when a current architecture diagram looks modular.
How unstable boundaries increase cognitive load, concentrate ownership, and make scaling harder.
believe: Architecture must preserve enough stability for people to understand and share responsibility for AI-built systems.
Human workload belongs in the assessment of sustainable delivery speed.
can_do: Recognize temporal instability and identify domain boundaries, API contracts, and data-model decisions that need deliberate change control.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader distinguishes the Vibe Monolith from the classic, distributed, and release monoliths, and from under-refactoring.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What makes the Vibe Monolith distinct if its components look modular today?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Its architecture and boundaries keep moving, preventing people from reasoning about one part over time; this differs from a single application, static cross-service coupling, release coordination, and duplication caused by under-refactoring.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader connects moving boundaries to cognitive load, concentrated ownership, burnout, and the difficulty of scaling beyond a small team.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How does architectural instability create a human cost, especially for people fluent with AI?
acceptance_criteria.expected: People cannot rely on stable seams or share lasting ownership, so responsibility concentrates on those who can still hold the whole system in mind; validation load rises and individual speed fails to remove coordination limits.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader names a concrete way to stabilize high-impact seams while allowing changes within them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What should a team hold stable, and what first action follows from the article?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Domain boundaries, API contracts, and the data model need deliberate decisions and review; record them, gate changes to them, track churn and review burden, or use a focused architecture forum while allowing work inside the boundaries.

thesis.question: How can teams sustain AI-assisted development when the architecture changes faster than people can understand and own it?
thesis.claim: Teams should stabilize domain boundaries, API contracts, and data models while allowing fast changes within them, because continuous re-architecting destroys shared ownership and concentrates validation work on a few engineers.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that repeated end-to-end regeneration and enough after-the-fact testing can sustain rapid development without deliberately holding architectural boundaries stable.
thesis.so_what: Architecture decisions determine whether increased output can scale across teams without exhausting the people who understand the system.
thesis.how_why: When boundaries keep moving, local reasoning and durable ownership fail; the few people able to follow the whole system inherit the coordination and validation burden, while stable seams make that work divisible.

role.contribution: Shows how architecture can protect and distribute the understanding that the preceding essay says people must retain.

transition_in.carries_over: People must understand generated work well enough to maintain it and judge its value.
transition_in.introduces: Stable architectural seams that make such understanding and ownership possible across a growing team.

posts.title: Can RISC-Inspired Platforms Make AI Less Risky?
posts.question: When can reducing a software platform make AI-assisted development easier to trust?

know: How the RISC analogy applies to the changing platform surface shared by coding agents and human reviewers.
Why lower generation cost changes, but does not settle, reuse-versus-local-code decisions.
believe: The smallest reliable platform is preferable when it lowers total understanding and ownership burden.
Reduction must preserve evaluation, operational safeguards, and mature expertise where they are needed.
can_do: Choose between reuse and generated local code using scope, edge cases, failure consequences, inspectability, and ownership.
Identify the risks of local-code sprawl, false confidence, fragmentation, and displaced complexity.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains RISC and the platform analogy in terms of both agent and reviewer understanding.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What does RISC mean here, and what is the software equivalent of an instruction set?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Reduced Instruction Set Computer supplies an analogy for a smaller, regular surface; frameworks, APIs, dependencies, conventions, and local code form a changing platform that both agents and humans must understand, with text files, tests, diffs, and version control as inspectable examples.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader makes a bounded reuse-versus-generation decision without concluding that fewer dependencies are always better.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How would the article compare generating a narrow local helper with replacing a mature security-sensitive library?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The helper may be appropriate if small, testable, locally recoverable, and owned; mature high-risk implementations retain expertise and edge-case coverage. Compare total review, operation, and maintenance burden rather than line count or generation speed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader connects reduction to evaluation and stewardship, including risks created by excessive reduction.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What must accompany a reduced platform so that local simplicity does not create a new problem?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tests, observable failure behavior, review and ownership, shared primitives or examples, and checks for fragmentation, missed edge cases, false confidence, sprawl, and complexity moved into operations or hidden knowledge.

thesis.question: When can reducing a software platform make AI-assisted development easier to trust?
thesis.claim: Reducing the platform surface can make AI-generated systems easier to trust when it exposes behavior for joint human and agent review while preserving mature abstractions whose expertise and safeguards outweigh their complexity.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that broad frameworks and dependency reuse remain the default answer because saving implementation effort outweighs the added review surface even when generation is cheap.
thesis.so_what: Platform and dependency choices should be judged by how well the team can evaluate, operate, and own the result, not only by how quickly a model can generate it.
thesis.how_why: Fewer hidden behaviors lower the effort of tracing changes and failures, but local replacements also create edge-case and maintenance obligations; evaluation and stewardship determine which choice reduces the total burden.

role.contribution: Turns stable seams into a platform strategy that reduces the amount of hidden behavior agents and reviewers must reason about.

transition_in.carries_over: Stable seams let teams reason locally and share ownership of an AI-built system.
transition_in.introduces: How to keep the platform inside those seams inspectable without discarding expertise or operational safeguards.

know: How changing models alter the product itself rather than only its development process.
believe: Repeated evaluation of customer fit should govern product change even when model benchmarks improve.
can_do: Separate a stable customer promise from assumptions that must be revisited when model capability changes.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can explain why a product may need reinterpretation and why new capability alone cannot justify it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What should remain stable, and what should be re-evaluated when the model behind a product changes?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Preserve the customer promise and trust commitments; re-evaluate workflows, controls, model assumptions, quality, cost, and customer/business outcomes before committing.

thesis.question: What changes in product management when a generative model is part of the product's material?
thesis.claim: Model-powered products require recurring reassessment of workflows and value hypotheses as models change, with evaluation of customer fit and a stable product promise governing what gets rebuilt.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that ordinary feature planning plus adoption of higher-performing model versions is sufficient, because improving model capability will improve the product in place.
thesis.so_what: Product teams need to budget for discovery, comparison, migration, and selective retirement rather than count faster implementation as product progress.
thesis.how_why: Model releases can change available interactions and regress valued behavior simultaneously, while customer preferences and real workflow use determine whether the new possibilities create value.

supporting_claims.claim: Changing model material can make current workflows obsolete or regress their fit even as general capability improves.
Customer evidence, evaluation, and a stable product promise distinguish deliberate seasonal change from novelty chasing.

role.contribution: Extends the software discussion from producing a system to preserving customer value when its model-dependent behavior changes.

transition_in.carries_over: The software part establishes inspectable platforms, intended behavior, and evaluation for AI-assisted building.
transition_in.introduces: When the model is in the customer product, the behavior and product assumptions themselves can change between model releases.

flow.rationale: This part has one essay, so there is no internal post order to change. Keeping the distinction between development tools and product material in a separate part prevents the seasonal-product recommendation from being read as a rule that every software team must rebuild continuously.

hook.content: When a new model arrives, does it merely help the team build, or does it change what the product should be?

opening.bridge: Use the distinction between AI-assisted development and model-powered products to show why cheaper implementation is no longer the whole planning problem.
opening.roadmap: Explain the changing material, then the seasonal operating rhythm, the evaluation that selects changes, and the product promise that survives them.

closing.synthesis: A stable promise and a changing implementation can coexist when each model-driven change is evaluated as a customer-value bet.
closing.so_what: Fast rebuilding matters only when teams can tell whether the resulting product still serves its users.
closing.callback: The opening distinction between a better development tool and a change to the product material.

takeaway.content: Treat model upgrades as evaluated product changes, preserving user jobs and trust while testing which new workflows deserve release.

posts.title: Software Has Seasons Now: Fashion-Driven Development for Generative AI Products
posts.question: How should product teams plan when generative models are part of the product and keep changing?

know: The difference between using AI to develop software and building a product whose value depends on models.
Why model changes can require seasonal product reinterpretation and can regress local fit despite higher general capability.
believe: Outcome-focused product management needs explicit model assumptions, repeated evaluation, and a stable customer promise.
Model novelty and benchmarks do not establish customer or business value.
can_do: Frame a model-driven change as a testable bet with a value hypothesis, preserved promise, regression checks, and a ship, delay, retire, or revert decision.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader distinguishes AI-assisted delivery from model-powered products and explains what seasonal change adds to outcome-focused product management.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Why does a new model create a different problem for an AI-powered product than for a team using AI to write code?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The model changes the product's material, possible workflows, customer expectations, and failure modes; discovery and planning must revisit model assumptions and product fit while retaining the existing focus on outcomes.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader explains why a stronger model is not automatically an upgrade for a particular product.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A new model scores higher on general benchmarks. What could still make switching to it wrong for this product?
acceptance_criteria.expected: It may regress representative user jobs, expert control, tone or consistency, safety boundaries, latency, costs, or the product promise; customer behavior and fit cannot be inferred from benchmark rank.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader describes an evaluation-led seasonal decision that preserves the customer promise and separates exploration from commitment.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How should a team decide what to preserve, rebuild, retire, or test after a model changes?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Scout the change, state a customer-value hypothesis and stable promise, compare old and new on representative scenarios and customer/business evidence, use stop conditions, and archive the decision; release selectively rather than chase every model.

thesis.question: How should product teams plan when generative models are part of the product and keep changing?
thesis.claim: Model-powered product teams should plan recurring, evaluation-led reinterpretations of workflows around changing models while preserving a stable customer promise, because a new model can enable previously infeasible workflows while breaking behavior that an existing customer job depends on.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that model releases are chiefly component upgrades within a stable feature roadmap, so benchmark improvements justify adoption without reconsidering workflows and customer fit.
thesis.so_what: Roadmaps, discovery, briefs, and release decisions need explicit model assumptions and customer evidence so that repeated rebuilds protect value rather than follow novelty.
thesis.how_why: A model change can remove workflow constraints and introduce new failure modes at once; only comparison on real user jobs, controls, trust boundaries, cost, and business outcomes shows which changes deserve commitment.

role.contribution: Extends the journal's outcome and evaluation discipline to products whose own behavior changes with the model material.

know: How explicit intent and bounded delegation make AI assistance usable without transferring human responsibility.
How agency, judgment, and persuasion turn generated options into action people can support.
believe: More capable AI calls for clearer accountability and deliberate leadership practice.
can_do: Set an appropriate interaction boundary and practice the human capabilities needed to use the result.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader connects a bounded AI workflow to the human decisions and relationships needed to make its output useful.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What remains for a leader after AI produces options and can execute within a spec?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Set intent and permissions, verify competence, decide trade-offs in context, retain ownership, initiate responsible action, and gain the understanding and support of affected people.

thesis.question: What must leaders do differently when AI can propose and execute more of the work?
thesis.claim: Leaders should make intent and delegation boundaries explicit and practice agency, contextual judgment, and persuasion, because AI-generated artifacts and autonomous execution do not transfer accountability or earn people's commitment.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that leaders mainly need greater prompt fluency and wider automation to preserve their contribution as AI takes over analysis and artifact production.
thesis.so_what: Leadership development should be judged by accountable decisions and shared action, not by the quantity or polish of generated plans.
thesis.how_why: A model can prepare options and act within permissions, but legitimate goals, acceptable trade-offs, trust, and consent depend on people who understand the context and live with the consequences.

supporting_claims.claim: Intent statements and specs make the outcome, context, constraints, and review expectations inspectable before AI acts.
AI autonomy should expand only with demonstrated competence, bounded control, and visible human responsibility.
Agency, contextual judgment, and persuasion remain necessary to turn AI-supported preparation into accountable action.

role.contribution: Names the human operating boundaries and capabilities needed to apply the preceding engineering and product disciplines.

transition_in.carries_over: Product change needs deliberate decisions about value, trust, and what should remain stable.
transition_in.introduces: The leadership language, delegation boundaries, and personal capabilities required to make and carry those decisions.

flow.rationale: The ladder first makes one human-AI interaction concrete: intent, scope, evidence, and review. The closing essay then widens from that interaction to initiating change, deciding in context, and aligning people across technical leadership roles. Reversing them would give an abstract skills prescription before showing the everyday decisions and boundaries in which those skills are exercised.

hook.content: When AI can do more than a small task, what intent, boundaries, and review does the work require?

opening.bridge: Start with familiar command prompts and show why consequential work needs a visible agreement rather than an implied transfer of judgment.
opening.roadmap: First choose and govern a level of human-AI collaboration; then develop the agency, judgment, and persuasion that turn its output into action.

closing.synthesis: Explicit intent makes AI work reviewable, while agency, judgment, and persuasion carry the resulting decisions into a real organization.
closing.so_what: The value of generated plans depends on people willing and able to own their consequences and align others around them.
closing.callback: The question of what leadership adds when the artifacts themselves can be generated.

takeaway.content: Use one real decision to practice stating intent, comparing and rejecting options, and explaining the chosen path to affected people.

posts.title: From Prompting to Intent: The Leadership Ladder for Working with AI
posts.question: How should leaders change their interaction with AI as it moves from narrow tasks to longer and more consequential workflows?

know: How Marquet's intent-based leadership supplies language for human-AI collaboration without giving AI human accountability.
How the seven interaction levels differ and why higher autonomy requires stronger evidence and boundaries.
believe: The right interaction level depends on ambiguity, consequences, and demonstrated competence rather than a desire to maximize autonomy.
can_do: Rewrite a consequential command as an intent statement or spec with context, constraints, evaluation, review, and stop conditions.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader chooses an interaction level appropriate to the work and rejects the idea that higher autonomy is always better.
acceptance_criteria.probe: How would you choose a level for formatting notes versus an agent changing an important workflow?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A command is sufficient for narrow, low-risk, easily checked work; ambiguous or consequential work needs explicit intent, competence evidence, limited permissions, review, and escalation before bounded delegation or monitored autonomy.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can turn a command into an inspectable agreement about the intended outcome and permitted action.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What would you add to "review this plan" to make it an intent-based collaboration, and when would you write a spec?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Name the decision, context, constraints, options, success criteria, allowed actions, review points, and stop conditions; consequential work merits a written contract that people can evaluate before and after AI acts.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader preserves human accountability while applying the leadership analogy and scaling guardrails.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What cannot be transferred to AI when moving up the ladder, and what controls must increase?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Humans retain purpose, legitimate trade-offs, approval, trust, and consequences; greater autonomy requires scope, competence checks, observable actions, review, escalation, rollback, and a named owner.

thesis.question: How should leaders change their interaction with AI as it moves from narrow tasks to longer and more consequential workflows?
thesis.claim: Leaders should move from commands to explicit intent, bounded delegation, and evidence-based autonomy as work demands it, while retaining human accountability and increasing review and control with each increase in autonomy.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that more capable agents chiefly need better prompts and broader permissions, and that polished output is sufficient evidence that the underlying judgment has been delegated.
thesis.so_what: Consequential AI work needs an inspectable agreement about goals, constraints, evaluation, and escalation before execution, so leaders can use agent capability without hiding the human decision.
thesis.how_why: Commands omit context and legitimate trade-offs; intent statements and specs expose those choices, while competence evidence, boundaries, and review keep execution proportional to what the organization can verify.

role.contribution: Makes the journal's requirement for human responsibility operational through language, specifications, and bounded autonomy.

posts.title: AI Will Do the Heavy Lifting. You Still Need to Lead
posts.question: Which capabilities should technology leaders practice as AI takes over more artifact production?

know: What agency, judgment, and persuasion contribute to technology leadership as artifacts become easier to produce.
Where AI support ends and human direction, accountability, consent, and trust remain.
believe: Leaders should practice initiating, choosing, and aligning people, while retaining technical fundamentals and adapting their practices as AI changes.
can_do: Identify a missing leadership capability in an AI-assisted decision and practice it through a bounded weekly exercise.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader distinguishes agency, judgment, and persuasion and identifies the consequence of missing each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What are the three capabilities, and how can AI-assisted leadership fail when each is missing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Agency initiates responsible action rather than waiting; judgment selects in local context rather than accepting plausible or fashionable output; persuasion makes decisions understandable and legitimate to people rather than leaving them unsupported.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader separates AI-supported preparation from the leadership responsibilities that remain human.
acceptance_criteria.probe: If AI can produce plans, options, and persuasive messages, what does a technology leader still own?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Choosing direction and acceptable trade-offs, understanding local capacity and history, taking responsibility, earning trust, and aligning people; generated artifacts do not transfer accountability or consent.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can name a practical learning loop relevant to their role without discarding technical fundamentals.
acceptance_criteria.probe: What would you practice this week, and how should that practice change as AI capability evolves?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Use a real decision, compare options, reject one with contextual reasons, test risks, translate for a stakeholder, and seek peer feedback; keep technical foundations while adjusting how agency, judgment, and persuasion are exercised.

thesis.question: Which capabilities should technology leaders practice as AI takes over more artifact production?
thesis.claim: Technology leaders should prioritize agency, contextual judgment, and persuasion because generating options does not initiate responsible change, choose legitimate trade-offs, or earn the trust required to act on them.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that technical leaders can preserve their contribution mainly by becoming faster producers of diagrams, plans, and recommendations with AI tools.
thesis.so_what: Career development and daily leadership practice should emphasize accountable decisions and alignment across people, while preserving the technical knowledge those decisions rely on.
thesis.how_why: AI expands the supply of plausible artifacts, but turning an artifact into an outcome still requires someone to start, choose in context, and gain commitment from the people affected.

role.contribution: Closes the collection by showing the human capabilities needed to carry stated intent through evaluation into accountable action.

transition_in.carries_over: Intent-based collaboration defines the boundaries and evidence needed for AI-assisted work.
transition_in.introduces: The agency, contextual judgment, and persuasion people must practice to set those boundaries and turn outputs into shared decisions.
